briefs.working_title: Lawn Fertilizer Near Palm Trees: A Southwest Florida Warning
secondary_kws: can lawn fertilizer kill palm trees
how far do palm tree roots spread
briefs.intent: informational explainer (Waves Pest Insider fact P03 in pest-insider-facts-v1: the roots of large palms typically reach 50 feet or more from the trunk, and high-nitrogen lawn fertilizer, even 30 feet away, has been known to kill palms by triggering potassium deficiency)
briefs.thesis: UF/IFAS says the roots of large palms typically extend out 50 feet or more from the trunk in all directions and take up whatever fertilizers have been applied to the turfgrass. UF/IFAS says most turf fertilizers have a high ratio of nitrogen to potassium and no magnesium, which forces rapid growth in a palm without enough potassium or magnesium to support it, and that this brings on or worsens potassium and magnesium deficiencies. UF/IFAS says high-nitrogen fertilizers applied to turfgrass, even 30 feet away from a palm on one side only, have been known to kill palms from induced potassium deficiency. UF/IFAS recommends its palm maintenance fertilizer for the entire landscape, lawn included, which removes the problem.
outline: The short answer: lawn fertilizer can harm a palm that stands well away from the fertilized grass; UF/IFAS says the roots of large palms typically extend out 50 feet or more from the trunk in all directions and take up whatever fertilizers have been applied to the turfgrass, and that high-nitrogen fertilizers applied to turfgrass, even 30 feet away from a palm on one side only, have been known to kill palms from induced potassium deficiency; state this fact in one passage with both distances, as the first verify note requires

How far the roots of a palm reach: UF/IFAS says roots of large palms typically extend out 50 feet or more from the trunk in all directions; UF/IFAS gives the example of a large palm relatively close to a property line, where the fertilizer a neighbor puts on his lawn is within the area covered by the root system of the palm; give no other distance and say nothing about root depth

Why lawn fertilizer hurts a palm: UF/IFAS says the high ratio of nitrogen to potassium and the lack of any magnesium in most turf fertilizers force rapid growth in palms; without sufficient potassium or magnesium to support that growth, the growth dilutes the potassium and magnesium reserves within the palm and induces or worsens potassium and magnesium deficiencies; UF/IFAS adds that, given the high value of most specimen palms, applying high-nitrogen fertilizers to palms or to nearby turfgrass is no bargain; name no fertilizer product and give no analysis numbers

What a palm short of potassium looks like: UF/IFAS says symptoms of potassium deficiency vary among species but always appear first on the oldest leaves; in many palms the early symptoms are translucent yellow or orange spots on the leaflets, and as the deficiency progresses the leaflet margins and tips die; in severe cases the canopy holds only a few leaves, all of them yellowed, frizzled and stunted, the trunk begins to taper, and death of the palm often follows; UF/IFAS says potassium is readily leached from sand and limestone soils, and that this deficiency is very common on palms grown in highly leached sandy soils

What UF/IFAS recommends in a yard with palms and grass: UF/IFAS recommends its palm maintenance fertilizer for use on the entire landscape, and says this simplifies fertilizing to a single product and eliminates the problem of high-nitrogen turf fertilizers near palms; UF/IFAS says palms need more nutrients than other types of plants, so a fertilizer that is suitable for palms is more than suitable for the others; in comparative trials at a UF/IFAS research center, St. Augustinegrass fertilized with the palm maintenance fertilizer had quality equal to that produced by a high quality turf fertilizer; describe the fertilizer only as the palm maintenance fertilizer in the UF/IFAS guide and link the guide; give no analysis numbers, no product name and no rate

Summer fertilizer rules in our area: UF/IFAS notes that in some Florida counties or municipalities all fertilizers that contain nitrogen and phosphorus may be prohibited during the rainy months of June through September, and describes palm fertilizers with no nitrogen or phosphorus for that period; UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says that from June 1 to September 30 no fertilizer containing nitrogen or phosphorus should be applied to turf or landscape plants in Sarasota County, and that Venice has adopted and follows the Sarasota County ordinance; the same page says North Port has its own ordinance with its own restriction period, which this post does not state; check your county or city rules before you fertilize (link /lawn-care/fertilizer-blackout-sarasota-county/ and /lawn-care/fertilizer-blackout-manatee-county/ and /lawn-care/north-port-fertilizer-blackout-april-start/)

When the fertilizer is not yours to choose: UF/IFAS says a neighbor who fertilizes his lawn with typical turf fertilizers will negatively affect the health of a large palm close to the property line; UF/IFAS says a study showed that when the turfgrass near a palm has been fertilized with a typical turf fertilizer, the negative effects can be prevented by fertilizing the area under the canopy of the palm with a palm fertilizer that has no nitrogen or phosphorus; a practical step, which is ours and not from UF/IFAS: find out what is applied to the grass near your palms, and tell whoever fertilizes the lawn that the palms are there; UF/IFAS says to contact your county Extension agent for information about the availability of these palm fertilizers in your area; give no rate and no application steps

How long a palm takes to recover: UF/IFAS says nutrient deficiencies are more easily prevented than corrected once they occur, that correction can take as long as 2 or 3 years for some elements, and that treatment of potassium-deficient palms typically requires from one to three years or longer, since the entire canopy of the palm has to be replaced with new, symptom-free leaves; promise no recovery

What Waves does and does not do: the Waves lawn program covers turf fertility, weed, insect and disease control, and diagnosis of lawn problems; tree and shrub care is a separate Waves service, and this post does not describe what it includes or applies; if you have palms in or near the lawn, say so when you ask for an estimate; link the tree and shrub care pages for Sarasota and Bradenton (link /tree-and-shrub-care-sarasota-fl/ and /tree-and-shrub-care-bradenton-fl/); for a question about one palm, your county UF/IFAS Extension office is the public place to ask; call to action: link "Request a Tree and Shrub Care Estimate" to /contact/

the guide describes palm fertilizers with no nitrogen or phosphorus, and a study in which palms that got such a fertilizer for the summer application had quality as good as palms that got a nitrogen-containing palm fertilizer for all applications; readers are told to contact their county Extension agent for information about the availability of these products in their area; palm nutritional requirements are higher than those for other types of plants, so a fertilizer that is suitable for palms will be more than suitable for other types of plants; comparative trials at a UF/IFAS research and education center have shown that St. Augustinegrass fertilized with the palm maintenance fertilizer had quality equal to that produced by a high quality turf fertilizer; use of the palm maintenance fertilizer is recommended for the entire landscape, which simplifies fertilization to a single product and eliminates a serious problem encountered when high-nitrogen turf fertilizers are applied to turf areas with palms growing nearby; roots of large palms typically extend out 50 feet or more from the trunk in all directions and will take up whatever fertilizers have been applied to the turfgrass; the high ratio of nitrogen to potassium and the lack of any magnesium in most turf fertilizers forces rapid growth in palms, but without sufficient potassium or magnesium to support that growth, the growth dilutes the existing potassium and magnesium reserves within the palm and induces or exacerbates potassium and magnesium deficiencies; high-nitrogen fertilizers applied to turfgrass, even 30 feet away from a palm on one side only, have been known to kill palms from induced potassium deficiency; given the high value of most specimen palms, applying high-nitrogen fertilizers to the palms or to nearby turfgrass is no bargain; sometimes it may not be possible to control what kinds of fertilizer are applied within the area covered by the root system of a palm, for example a large palm relatively close to a property line, where a neighbor may be fertilizing his lawn with typical turf fertilizers that will negatively affect the health of the palm; a study has shown that if the turfgrass near a palm has been fertilized with a typical turf fertilizer, the negative impacts can be prevented by fertilizing the area under the canopy of the palm with the palm fertilizer that has no nitrogen or phosphorus; EP269 is the UF/IFAS publication on potassium deficiency in palms (ENH1017, original September 2005, revised May 2011, reviewed April 2020). Attribute it as UF/IFAS. It gives fertilizer products, analysis numbers and rates: take none of those, and do not use its treatment time span in this post. Verified statements: symptoms of potassium deficiency vary among species, but always appear first on the oldest leaves; in most palms other than the ones it describes one by one, early symptoms appear as translucent yellow or orange spotting on the leaflets, and as the deficiency progresses, marginal and tip necrosis will also be present; in severe cases the canopy will contain only a few leaves, all of which will be chlorotic, frizzled and stunted, the trunk will begin to taper, and death of the palm often follows; potassium deficiency is caused by insufficient potassium in the soil, but can be induced or accentuated by a high ratio of nitrogen to potassium in the soil; potassium is readily leached from sand or limestone soils; potassium deficiency is very common on palms grown in highly leached sandy soils.

Sarasota County source: the UF/IFAS Extension Sarasota County page on fertilizer management (last modified August 13, 2026). Attribute it as UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County. briefs.primary_kw: why weeds keep coming back in lawn

briefs.intent: informational explainer (Waves Pest Insider fact L11 in pest-insider-facts-v1: weeds are a sign of weakened turf, not the cause, and healthy turf shades the soil so sunlight cannot reach weed seeds)
briefs.thesis: Weeds are a symptom. UF/IFAS says the presence of weeds is a result of a weakened turfgrass stand, not the cause of it, and that healthy turf shades the soil so sunlight cannot reach weed seeds ready to germinate. In its words, weeds do not create a void; they fill a void. Where weeds keep returning, UF/IFAS points to turf that is thin, weak or open, and it names what weakens turf: mistakes in watering, fertilizing and mowing, traffic and compacted soil, shade, and damage from insects, disease and nematodes. Unless those factors are corrected, UF/IFAS says continued weed encroachment should be expected.
outline: The short answer: weeds keep coming back where the grass is thin or weak; UF/IFAS says the presence of weeds is a result of a weakened turfgrass stand, not the cause of it, and that healthy turf shades the soil so sunlight cannot reach weed seeds ready to germinate; state this fact in one passage, as the first verify note requires

Weeds fill a gap that is already there: UF/IFAS says it is the lack of proper turf density, the voids in the turf and any open areas that let light reach the soil surface that promote weed encroachment; a thick turf also minimizes the physical space available for weeds to become established; UF/IFAS says it is very important to understand that weeds do not create a void, they fill a void

Watering, fertilizer and mowing: UF/IFAS says proper fertilization, watering and mowing are required to produce a dense turf that can prevent weed infestation; if turf is overwatered or underwatered, overfertilized or underfertilized, or mowed too low or too infrequently, the turf is weakened and weeds move in; UF/IFAS says sharpening the mower blades can reduce turf damage and the chances for weed invasion; give no mowing height and no watering amount here, and link the Waves blog posts that cover them (link /lawn-care/mowing-height-by-grass-type/ and /lawn-care/overwatering-lawn-vs-underwatering/)

Traffic, compaction and wet soil: UF/IFAS says turf damaged by foot or vehicle traffic invites weeds, and that turf growing in soil compacted by excessive traffic cannot develop a healthy root system as well as it can in soil that is not compacted; UF/IFAS says goosegrass, annual bluegrass, dollarweed and certain sedges grow well in compacted or continuously wet soil, and that to manage weeds there, the compaction or the wet condition should be dealt with (link /lawn-care/types-of-weeds-bradenton-fl/)

Too much shade for grass: UF/IFAS says growing bermudagrass or bahiagrass under any shade results in thin, weak turf that is very susceptible to weed invasion; UF/IFAS says no grasses perform well in heavily shaded areas, and that an alternative to turf, such as a groundcover, should be considered there

Insects, disease and nematodes: UF/IFAS says pest damage makes turf more susceptible to weed infestations by creating spaces for weeds and reducing the ability of the turf to compete; tunneling from mole crickets disrupts the soil surface, which lets weed seeds germinate readily; other insects and diseases can cause areas of turf to become bare, and these open areas are usually slow to recover; high nematode populations also thin the turf, and UF/IFAS says weeds that often become established in nematode-infested soil include spotted spurge and Florida pusley

Weeds that arrive from the edges: UF/IFAS says areas next to a lawn that are hard to mow, such as fence rows or ditch banks, often support a weed population that normally produces seed that infests the nearby turf, and that these areas should also get weed management attention; UF/IFAS calls it a good practice to wash off mowers and trimmers used in weed-infested areas before mowing or trimming in weed-free areas

Why a weed treatment alone does not end it: UF/IFAS says successful weed control starts with healthy, dense turf, and that unless the factors behind the weak turf are corrected, continued weed encroachment should be expected; UF/IFAS describes weed management as an integrated approach in which success may depend on multiple years of patient work on a carefully planned strategy; so a weed treatment deals with the weeds that are there, and the cause of the thin turf still has to be corrected (link /lawn-care/pre-emergent-weed-control-lakewood-ranch-fl/ and /lawn-care/post-emergent-herbicides-lakewood-ranch-fl/)

What Waves does and does not do: the Waves lawn program covers turf fertility, weed, insect and disease control, and diagnosis of lawn problems; it does not include mowing or irrigation repair, which Waves refers to a landscaper or an irrigation contractor; link the lawn care pages for Sarasota and Bradenton (link /lawn-care-sarasota-fl/ and /lawn-care-bradenton-fl/); to have a lawn with returning weeds looked at, call to action: link "Request a Lawn Weed Control Estimate" to /contact/

briefs.working_title: Yellow Lawn After Spring Fertilizer in Southwest Florida
secondary_kws: yellow patches in St. Augustine grass in spring
briefs.intent: informational explainer (Waves Pest Insider fact L07 in pest-insider-facts-v1: iron deficiency is common in Florida lawns in spring after a nitrogen feeding, and it usually fades within a few weeks)
briefs.thesis: Yellow areas in a lawn after a spring feeding are a known pattern in Florida. UF/IFAS says iron deficiency is commonly observed in Florida in the spring following nitrogen fertilizer applications, especially on bahiagrass, centipedegrass and St. Augustinegrass. UF/IFAS gives the most likely explanation: the nitrogen encourages growth and raises the demand for iron, but root growth is still limited in the spring, so the grass cannot take up enough iron and the leaf blades lose their green color. UF/IFAS says springtime occurrences of iron deficiency normally dissipate within a few weeks, as soil temperatures rise and the roots grow. Iron and nitrogen are not interchangeable: UF/IFAS says an application of iron will not cure a nitrogen deficiency.
outline: The short answer: UF/IFAS says iron deficiency is commonly observed in Florida in the spring following nitrogen fertilizer applications, especially on bahiagrass, centipedegrass and St. Augustinegrass, and that springtime occurrences of iron deficiency normally dissipate within a few weeks; state this fact in one passage, as the first verify note requires

Why feeding can turn a lawn yellow in spring: UF/IFAS gives what it calls the most likely explanation: during the winter months the rate of turfgrass shoot and root growth declines, and in south Florida growth may slow down; nitrogen applied during the spring encourages growth and, in turn, increases the demand for iron; that demand cannot be met because root growth is still limited in the spring, so the leaf blades become chlorotic, which a homeowner sees as yellowing; UF/IFAS says this can be frustrating, because the nitrogen should have produced greener grass, and that cool, wet soils tend to make this chlorosis worse
Where it shows up first: UF/IFAS says iron is immobile in the plant, so iron deficiency appears on the younger leaves first; UF/IFAS says the lawn may appear chlorotic in places

briefs.thesis: On a palm that is short of potassium, the discolored fronds at the bottom are the ones to leave on. If they are removed, the palm then removes potassium from the next leaves up, which are currently green and symptom free. Completely dead leaves are a different case: UF/IFAS says removing them is never a problem.

What happens when they are cut off: UF/IFAS says that if the older discolored leaves are removed, the palm then removes potassium from the next leaves up, which are currently green and symptom free; UF/IFAS says repeated pruning of potassium-deficient older leaves has been shown to reduce the number of green, symptom-free leaves in the canopy and, in severely potassium-deficient palms, is known to accelerate the rate of decline leading to death of the palm

When an old frond is just old: UF/IFAS describes natural aging on palms that have a crownshaft: a healthy old leaf is completely green one day, completely orange-brown the second day and completely brown the third day, when it should fall off by itself; UF/IFAS says half-dead old leaves that remain on the palm for months at a time are usually deficient in potassium

What can be pruned: UF/IFAS says removal of completely dead leaves and of flower and fruit stalks from palms is never a problem; UF/IFAS says a properly fertilized and pruned palm should have a round canopy with green leaves right down to the bottom; UF/IFAS cites a pruning standard for palms which states that no leaves with tips above the horizontal plane, the 9:00 and 3:00 positions on a clock face, should be removed; UF/IFAS says palm pruning is done primarily for aesthetic purposes; fronds that touch a roof are a separate question that the Waves blog covers (link /pest-control/palm-fronds-touching-roof-rats/)

briefs.intent: informational explainer (Waves Pest Insider fact P05 in pest-insider-facts-v1: lethal bronzing lives only in the sap of a palm or in an insect, so pruning tools cannot spread it, and a palm that shows symptoms and tests positive should be removed right away)
briefs.thesis: Lethal bronzing is a palm disease that UF/IFAS says was discovered in Florida in 2006. It is caused by a phytoplasma, a type of bacteria that lacks a cell wall. UF/IFAS says the phytoplasma is limited to the phloem, the sap, of the palm and cannot survive outside a plant or insect; therefore it cannot be mechanically transmitted, for example by pruning tools or by infected roots touching new roots. Insects that feed on the sap carry it from palm to palm. UF/IFAS says that once a palm shows symptoms and tests positive for the phytoplasma, it should be removed immediately. The UF/IFAS list of Florida counties with confirmed cases includes Manatee, Sarasota and Charlotte.
outline: The short answer: UF/IFAS says the organism behind lethal bronzing is limited to the phloem, the sap, of the palm and cannot survive outside a plant or insect, so it cannot be mechanically transmitted, for example by pruning tools or by infected roots touching new roots; UF/IFAS says that once a palm shows symptoms and tests positive, it should be removed immediately; state this fact in one passage, as the first verify note requires

How it spreads, and how it does not: UF/IFAS says phytoplasmas are transmitted to plants by piercing-sucking insects that feed on the sap, that the insects spread the phytoplasma from plant to plant as they feed on different hosts, and that planthoppers and leafhoppers are the main groups of insects that transmit phytoplasmas; UF/IFAS says phytoplasmas are not known to survive outside their host, whether the host is plant or insect, which is why pruning tools and roots that touch do not pass it on; name no insect species

The first signs to watch for: UF/IFAS says the first symptoms are variable; if fruit is present, the first symptom is generally premature fruit drop; if fruit has not set but flower stalks are present, they become necrotic, which means they die; UF/IFAS notes that these are not reliable indicators if the palm is not old enough to produce fruit, is not flowering at the time, or has had its flower stalks trimmed; this progresses to discoloration of the oldest leaves, those closest to the ground, which gradually advances to younger leaves; the final stage is the collapse of the spear leaf, which shows that the bud of the palm has died and there is no chance of saving the palm

How fast it moves: UF/IFAS says the length of time between infection and symptom development appears to be about four to five months, and that from symptom development to collapse of the spear leaf is about two to three months, but that this is highly variable; UF/IFAS says symptoms progress at different rates in different palm species; give no other time span

Which palms get it, and where: UF/IFAS says the phytoplasma has been found in 21 different species of palm, among them cabbage palm, queen palm, coconut palm, Canary Island date palm, pygmy date palm, Christmas palm and Bismarck palm; UF/IFAS says it has been isolated from palms in 36 Florida counties, and its list of counties with confirmed cases includes Manatee, Sarasota and Charlotte; UF/IFAS says that, to date, the disease is most prevalent in the central part of Florida but is spreading farther north and south; say that these counts come from the UF/IFAS publication as revised in June 2022

briefs.intent: informational explainer (Waves Pest Insider fact M02 in pest-insider-facts-v1: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus fly only a few blocks in their lifetime, but the black salt marsh mosquito has a long flight range and emerges in large numbers after rains and flooding)
briefs.thesis: How far a mosquito flies depends on which mosquito it is, and that decides what a homeowner can do about it. CDC says Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus do not fly long distances: in their lifetime, these mosquitoes will only fly a few blocks. They lay eggs on the inner walls of containers with water, so a mosquito of these two kinds comes from water within a few blocks of where it bites. The black salt marsh mosquito is the opposite case. UF/IFAS says its larval habitats are typically restricted to the coastal salt marshes, but the species has a long flight range and can be found far inland at times, and it emerges in large numbers after rains and flooding events. UF/IFAS says destroying container breeding sites will have a minimal effect on it, though the practice can reduce the numbers of other mosquito species found around a home.
